Obtain CT of the abdomen and pelvis in patients with moderate to severe signs and symptoms. C

Guidelines recommend against antibiotics in immunocompetent otherwise healthy patients with acute uncomplicated diverticulitis. They are recommended for immunocompromised patients and those with complicated acute diverticulitis (abscess, fistula, perforation, or stricture). B

Consider outpatient therapy in patients without intractable vomiting or signs of peritonitis and in patients for whom adequate follow-up is planned after 2 to 3 days of initiating antibiotic therapy. C
Consider surgery in patients who fail to respond to initial medical therapy or who have frequent recurrences; laparoscopic surgery results in a shorter length of stay and fewer complications. B
Current evidence does not support the standard recommendation that nut, corn, popcorn, and seed consumption should be avoided in patients with diverticular disease. B

The prevalence of a previously unsuspected colonic neoplasm is 8.3% in those with complicated diverticulitis, but less than 0.5% in those with uncomplicated diverticulitis. Guidelines recommend follow-up colonoscopy only if a first episode of uncomplicated diverticulitis or if complicated acute diveriticulitis. B

background.definition: Perforation or microperforation of a diverticulum occurs with subsequent infection and inflammation extending into the colon wall, epiploic appendages, mesentery, adjacent organs, or freely into the peritoneal cavity.

list.listitem: Diverticulosis was found in 20 to 100 per 1000 in autopsy and barium enema series in 1920 to 1940.
Diverticulitis affects 15% to 20% of patients with diverticulosis.
In 1998, there were 2.2 million cases of acute diverticulitis in the United States, accounting for $2.4 billion in health expenditures.
The yearly mortality rate in the United States from diverticular disease is 2.5 per 100,000 per year.
In 1996, it accounted for an estimated 3300 deaths in the United States.
Inflammation and infection in or around a diverticulum or localized perforation.
Risk factors for diverticulosis include inadequate dietary fiber and lack of physical activity (RR 1.6 for each).

Causes of diverticula include alterations in colonic wall resistance, colonic motility, and dietary factors such as lack of fiber, which contribute to increased intraluminal pressure and weakness of the bowel wall.
90% of diverticula are found in the sigmoid colon (left-sided) in Western societies. Right-sided diverticula are more common in Asian populations.
No screening tests are recommended. C
A high-fiber diet may prevent diverticular disease, while high red meat consumption and a Western style diet are associated with increased risk of diverticulitis. B
Increased physical activity is associated with lower risk of symptomatic diverticular disease. B
Obesity increases the risk of diverticulitis.
Current evidence does not support the standard recommendation that nut, corn, popcorn, and seed consumption should be avoided in patients with diverticular disease. B
Antibiotics and probiotics do not reduce the likelihood of recurrence.
ACP guidelines (2022) recommend against mesalamine based on 6 RCTs showing lack of benefit. A
Initial evaluation should include a problem-focused history, examination, CBC, urinalysis, and plain abdominal radiographs. C
Point of care ultrasound is highly accurate (LR+ 15, LR- 0.08) and is recommended if available, with CT a second choice. B
CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis should be considered to confirm the diagnosis and exclude complications, especially in patients with moderate to severe signs and symptoms. B

Colonoscopy is contraindicated in acute diverticulitis. It should be considered after 4 to 6 weeks to confirm the diagnosis and exclude other causes in patients with severe or complicated disease, C but not routinely following acute uncomplicated diverticulitis if not an initial episode. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, and abnormal abdominal X-rays
Diarrhea, weight loss, and mucus in stool
Pain out of proportion to examination findings
Weight loss, anemia, and GI bleeding
Flank pain, hematuria, and nephrolithiasis on abdominal X-rays

list.listitem: A problem-focused history and physical examination are recommended.

A small Swedish study found in 146 patients with clinically suspected acute diverticulitis that CT confirmed diverticulitis was more likely with younger age (OR 0.92), female sex (OR 4.8), LLQ pain (OR 15.1), and absence of vomiting (OR, 14.0). They propose a risk score based on a multivariate analysis but it has not been prospectively validated.

Patients present with left lower quadrant pain (93%–100%), fever and chills (57%–100%), nausea and vomiting, rectal mass, constipation, diarrhea, or urinary symptoms, rebound tenderness, and other peritoneal signs may be present with perforation and peritonitis.
Consider acute diverticulitis in the differential diagnosis (although less likely) in younger patients with abdominal pain and in older patients with right lower abdominal pain.

German national guidelines (2023) recommend that when acute diverticulitis is clinically suspected, a white blood cell count, C-reactive protein and urinalysis should be performed. They also recommend ultrasound or CT to confirm the diagnosis. While CT is more commonly used in the US, they argue that in good hands and with modern equipment diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound is high and radiation can be avoided for most patients. MRI is not routinely recommended.

US Infectious Disease Society of America (IDSA) guidelines recommend abdominal CT, ideally with contrast, as the initial test of choice for non-pregnant persons with suspected acute diverticulitis. Ultrasound or MRI are preferred in pregnant persons.
A systematic review concluded that point of care ultrasound is highly accurate (LR+ 15, LR- 0.08) and is recommended if available, with CT a second choice.
A systematic review found that c-reactive protein has good sensitivity (89% to 96%) but variable specificity, making it primarily useful to rule-out diverticulitis when < 10 mg/L.
Ultrasonography is preferred in women of childbearing age suspected of having diverticulitis.

Obtain a CBC as leukocytosis is present in about half of patients (54%). Order a urinalysis to rule out pyelonephritis, and order beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG; ) levels in premenopausal women to exclude pregnancy, and perform fecal occult blood test (FOBT) to exclude occult gastrointestinal bleeding.
Consider gram stain, and Clostridium difficile in patients with diarrhea.
Obtain an abdominal CT to confirm the diagnosis and exclude complications in patients with moderate to severe symptoms; CT may not be necessary in patients with mild symptoms.
A systematic review found a pooled sensitivity of 94% and specificity of 99% for the diagnosis of acute left-sided colonic diverticulitis with CT.
The CT findings best at ruling in diverticulitis are fascial thickening, inflamed diverticuli, free air, and the arrowhead sign. Absence of bowel thickening is strong evidence against diverticulitis.

The TICS protocol for point of care ultrasound stands for T (thickness of colon wall), I (intramural air present), C (colonic Murphy's sign which is tenderness with sonographic compression), and S (stranding of the pericolic fat). It was evaluated in 153 patients with clinically suspected diverticulitis, of whom half were ultimately diagnosed with it. The TICS protocol was 55% sensitive and 96% specific (LR+ 14.0, LR- 0.5) for diagnosis of complicated diverticulitis and 90% sensitive and 76% specific for diagnosis of simple diverticulitis (LR+ 3.8, LR- 0.12).

Colonoscopy and flexible sigmoidoscopy has limited use and should be avoided in the acute setting of diverticulitis. Patients with acute uncomplicated diverticulitis probably do not need colonoscopy, with a very low yield seen in a series of 1497 patients.

A systematic review of 17 studies with 3296 patients, including 959 with uncomplicated diverticulitis, found a 0.5% rate of colorectal cancer in patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis, compared with 8.3% in those with complicadted diverticulitis. Therefore, AGA guidelines (2021) and ACP guidelines (2022) both recommend colonoscopy 6 to 8 weeks following an episode of complicated diverticulitis. Patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis do not need colonoscopy if they have had a recent good quality colonoscopy, unless it is their first episode.
A clinical decision rule identified abdominal guarding, elevated c-reactive protein, and leukocytosis as independent predictors of complicated diverticulitis.
See the algorithm in for the diagnosis and treatment of acute diverticulitis.
See for a proposed staging system and the associated outcomes, based on a series of 631 patients.
Consider CT-guided percutaneous drainage for patients with diverticular abscess larger than 2 cm. B
Determine the need for hospitalization based on ability to tolerate oral intake, severity of illness, comorbid disease, and available outpatient support systems. C

Guidelines recommend against antibiotics in immunocompetent otherwise healthy patients with acute uncomplicated diverticulitis. They are recommended for immunocompromised patients and those with complicated acute diverticulitis (abscess, fistila, perforation, or stricture). B
Urgent sigmoid colectomy is required for patients with diffuse peritonitis or for those who fail nonoperative management of acute diverticulitis. B

Consider surgery in patients who fail to respond to initial medical therapy or who have frequent recurrences; laparoscopic surgery results in a shorter length of stay and fewer complications. Laparascopy with lavage and no resection is an option as well. B

Treatment of diverticulitis may involve IV fluids and limiting oral intake to clear liquids. American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) 2021 guidelines as well as American College of Physicians guidelines recommend against antibiotic for otherwise well immunocompetent persons with acute uncomplicated diverticulitis. They may be considered for patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis who are frail, have persistent or severe symptoms or vomiting, or have elevated inflammatory biomarkers (e.g. CRP > 150 mg/L). Antibiotics should be given to patients who have complicated diveriticulitis (perforation, obstruction, abscess, or fistula).
Italian guidelines (2024) similarly recommend no antibiotics for patients with uncomplicated acute diverticulitis in the absence of systemic illness, immunosuppression, or serious comorbidities.

A trial randomized 528 patients with CT proven left-sided uncomplicated acute diverticulitis to observation versus antibiotics, and found no statistically significant differences in outcomes (time to cure, need for surgery, recurrence, and mortality). However, all trends favored the antibiotic group. Observation is an option for stable patients with uncomplicated disease who do not wish to take antibiotics or who have a history of adverse effects with them.

A systematic review identified 7 studies with 2321 patients that compared antibiotics with observation alone, and found no difference in the likelihood of recurrence (11% vs 12%) or the need for emergency surgery (0.7% vs 1.4%). This review included non-randomized trials as well as randomized studies. The same study found that when looking at only RCTs, elective surgery was slightly more likely in those not receiving antibiotics (2.5% vs 0.9%, p = 0.04, NNT = 62). There was no difference in outcomes for oral vs IV antibiotics.
A second systematic review similarly found no clear benefit to antibiotics in patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis.

A third systematic review first used a Delphi process among patients and clinicians to identify clinically meaningful differences for the risk of persistent diverticulitis (4.0%), complicated diverticulitis (3.0%) and time to recovery (5 days faster). They then identified 3 RCTs and 6 observational studies comparing antibiotics with observation for acute uncomplicated diverticulitis and concluded that observation was non-inferior to antibiotics based on these non-inferiority margins.
A Cochrane review concluded that in uncomplicated diverticulitis, there is no evidence between a treatment strategy including antibiotics and on that does not.

If antibiotics are used, oral/outpatient regimens include: amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid 875 mg bid; sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim DS 1 bid PLUS metronidazole 500 mg tid; levofloxacin 750 mg daily or ciprofloxacin 750 mg bid PLUS metronidazole 500 mg tid.

Intravenous regimens include: piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g q6h or 4.5 g q8h; ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g q6h; ticarcillin-clavulanate 3.1 g q6h; moxifloxacin 400 mg q24h; ciprofloxacin 400 mg q12h or levofloxacin 750 mg q24h PLUS metronidazole 500 mg q6h or 1 g q12h.
Antibiotics should be renally dosed in patients with renal insufficiency.
There is one RCT (N = 51) that found no significant differences between IV cefoxitin versus IV gentamicin and clindamycin (RR 1.10, 95% CI, 0.85-1.30) in patients with acute diverticulitis.

ACP guidelines (2022) recommend against use of mesalamine to decrease the risk of recurrence based on a lack of efficacy in a meta-analysis of 6 randomized trials (absolute risk difference for recurrence between mesalamine and placebo 2.7% 95% CI, −1.6% to 7.5%).

Consider alternative diagnoses and surgical consultation for patients who fail to improve with conservative medical therapy. About 15% to 30% of patients admitted with acute diverticulitis will require surgery during that admission.
AGA and ACG guidelines recommend that patients with a complicated episode of acute diverticulitis or frequent recurrences consider surgical resection.

Italian guidelines (2024) recommend antibiotics with percutaneous drainage or surgery for patients with diverticulitis complicated by an abscess. They recommend antibiotics with surgery or laparascopic lavage in patients with perforation.
CT-guided percutaneous drainage is recommended for patients with a large diverticular abscess.

Laparoscopic colectomy compared to open colectomy has a shorter mean hospital stay (7.5 vs 9.4 days, P <.001) and lower overall complication rate (OR 0.64, 95% CI, 0.47-0.88), and decreased mortality among patients undergoing a primary anastomosis (vs colostomy).

Two trials have compared laparoscopic lavage (LL) with surgery for patients with purulent peritonitis due to diverticular perforation. The LADIES trial compared lavage with sigmoidectomy in 90 patients and found no difference in the primary endpoint of major morbidity or mortality in 12 months, or in mortality. Short-term, patients in the LL group had more in-hospital adverse events including the need for surgical intervention (18 vs 2 patients). Total medical costs were lower in the LL group, despite the need for more short-term interventions, due to the later need for stoma reversal in the comparison group. The DILALA study found no difference in mortality or readmission rates between 83 patients randomized to LL or colon resection with stoma. However, this study did find a lower rate of operations over 2 years, and no difference in short-term complications.

A meta-analysis found 3 trials comparing laparoscopic lavage (LL) with sigmoidectomy in patients with perforated diverticulitis and found similar rates of early reoperation and mortality, but higher rates of major complications (RR 1.7, 95% CI, 1.1-2.6). Resection and primary anastamosis had similar rates of mortality and major complications to Hartmann's procedure based on 3 studies with 255 patients. Patients undergoing primary anastamosis were less likely to have a stoma at 12 months, though. Another systematic review came to the same conclusion regarding resection with primary anastamosis compared with Hartmann's procedure.

A meta-analysis of 5 RCTs with 499 studies compared labaroscopic lavage (LL) with resection (n=3 studies) or Hartmann procedure (n=2) for perforated diverticulitis. Colonic resection had a lower likelihood of long-term ostomy (OR 0.02, 95% CI 0.003-0.20), incisional hernia (OR 0.184, 95% CI 0.10-0.33), long-term complications (OR 0.195, 95% CI 0.11-0.34), and eoperation (OR 0.2, 95% CI: 0.11-0.38). Patients randomized to LL had lower odds of reoperation (OR = 0.58, 95% CI 0.36-0.94) and long-term ostomy [OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.28-0.58] compared with those receiving colonic resection. However, the odds of recurrence of diverticular disease were higher (OR 5.8, 95% CI: 2.3-14.4).
Patients who smoked or who were using coriticosteroids were more likely to have a bad outcome following laparascopic lavage.
For patients with recurrent diverticulitis or who were persistently symptomatic, elective sigmoid resection improved quality of life and was cost-effective.
A Markov analysis found that the most cost-effective approach was to perform surgery only after the third episode of acute uncomplicated diverticulitis requiring hospitalization.
A randomized trial found that in patients with diverticulitis and extraluminal air seen on CT, surgery did not improve outcomes.

A meta-analysis of 11 observational studies with 2096 patients concluded that compared with early sigmoid resection, delayed resection had a potential benefit in terms of reduced conversion rates and shortened operative time, but with no difference in morbidity or mortality otherwise.
For outpatient treatment of diverticulitis, patients should start a clear liquid diet, oral broad-spectrum antiobiotics, and follow-up in 2 to 3 days.

The decision to hospitalize a patient with uncomplicated diverticulitis depends on several factors including the patient’s ability to tolerate oral intake, severity of illness, comorbid disease, and available outpatient support systems.
Consider hospitalization if patients have intractable vomiting, signs of peritonitis, or comorbid conditions (eg, immunocompromised state) or if adequate follow-up cannot be ensured.
Expect clinical improvement within 2 to 3 days to include decreasing fever, leukocytosis, and pain.
Complications include abscess, fistula, obstruction, phlegmon, bleeding, or perforation.
Patients who develop abscesses, usually larger than 2 cm, are candidates for percutaneous catheter drainage.

After percutaneous drainage of an abscess, later colectomy should be planned because 41% of patients will develop recurrent sepsis. Emergency surgery is required for patients with diffuse peritonitis or for those who fail nonoperative management of acute diverticulitis.

Chronic use of NSAIDs (OR 4.0, 95% CI, 2.1-7.6), corticosteroids (OR 5.7, 95% CI, 2.2-14.4), and opioid analgesics (OR 1.8, 95% CI, 1.1-3.0) are associated with colonic perforation in diverticular disease.
Immunocompromised patients are more likely to present with perforation or to fail medical management. Treatment often involves early surgical intervention.
Patients requiring hospitalization should be kept NPO; initiate IV fluids (normal saline or lactated Ringer’s solution) to restore intravascular volume, and start IV antiobiotics.

AGA guidelines (2021) and ACP guidelines (2022) both recommend colonoscopy 6 to 8 weeks following an episode of complicated diverticulitis. Patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis do not need colonoscopy if they have had a recent good quality colonoscopy, unless it is their first episode.
In a study involving 3165 patients treated for diverticulitis with a mean follow-up of 9 years, 9% had more than one recurrence. All recurrences were treated nonoperatively.
See for a staging system and prognosis, based on a series of 631 consecutive patients.
In a second study of 119 patients followed for 5 years, 97% of patients had minimal or no symptoms; only 2 had acute diverticulitis and 1 required surgery.
A large series (n = 1497) found malignancy in only 0.3% of patients with acute uncomplicated diverticulitis, a rate no different from that of the general population.

A systematic review of 17 studies with 3296 patients, including 959 with uncomplicated diverticulitis, found a 0.5% rate of colorectal cancer in patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis, compared with 8.3% in those with complicadted diverticulitis. A systematic review with 12 studies and 38,621 patients with diverticulitis found no long-term increase in the risk of colorectal cancer.

Among 2,214 patients (mean age 61) undergoing emergent surgery for colonic diverticulitis, the 30 day mortality was 5.1%; with worse mortality risk among those with renal dysfunction, hypoalbuminemia, worse ASA class and older age.
Recurrence is more likely in patients with complicated disease and in younger patients.
A German national guideline concluded that mortality risk is highest among patients with complicated diverticulitis, particularly if immunocompromised.
